title: How General Counsels Are Stepping Up as Unlikely AI Champions
author: Hope Cannon

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s augmentation and selective-deployment proposition, then concretely develops it for in-house governance and compliance. It identifies bounded recurring workflows, recommends phased expansion, and assigns GCs responsibility for secure, outcome-focused implementation, though its product-value claims are largely asserted rather than independently demonstrated.
qs: Automating the parts of the job that are repetitive or time-sensitive — and freeing up time for deeper thinking, analysis, and advice.
It means starting where AI can help most — board preparation, compliance tracking, or entity reporting — and building from there.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Cannon supports the cluster’s proposition that legal departments can capture AI gains when GC-led adoption targets recurring workflows and is integrated incrementally rather than treated as simple tool procurement. Her evidence reinforces the organisational-absorption bottleneck through the technology-roadmap gap and supports augmentation over replacement, though many claimed benefits are product-specific and not quantified.
qs: At the same time, three out of four legal departments admit they don’t yet have a technology roadmap.
It means starting where AI can help most — board preparation, compliance tracking, or entity reporting — and building from there.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that AI adoption should reshape legal-department workflows and roles rather than simply replace lawyers. It specifically endorses GC-led, secure and outcome-focused adoption that automates routine work and expands the department’s strategic contribution, while offering only illustrative—not measured—benefits. It does not materially address ALSPs, provider bargaining or pricing.
qs: As automation removes inefficiencies, and AI adds intelligence, legal departments evolve from operational hubs into strategic enablers.
GCs are in a unique position to shape how their organizations adopt AI: thoughtfully, securely, and with clear outcomes in mind.

kp.k: Reported AI adoption outpaces legal departments’ technology planning
kp.d: Cannon reports findings from FTI Consulting's The General Counsel Report 2025: more than two-thirds of GCs are open to generative AI for major legal use cases, nearly half report already using it, and three out of four legal departments lack a technology roadmap. The article frames this mismatch as both opportunity and risk; it provides no sample size or study methodology.
qs: According to FTI Consulting's The General Counsel Report 2025*, more than two-thirds of GCs are now open to using generative AI for major legal use cases — and nearly half say they’re already doing so.
At the same time, three out of four legal departments admit they don’t yet have a technology roadmap.
That gap between ambition and action is exactly where opportunity — and risk — sits.

kp.k: Expanding GC responsibilities encourage practical AI adoption
kp.d: Cannon links interest in AI to rising regulatory demands, greater board visibility, and pressure on in-house teams to manage complexity with fewer resources. She argues that successful adoption targets recurring operational problems rather than fashionable applications, with speed, accuracy and security as priorities.
qs: Today’s GCs are being asked to do more with less, manage more complexity with fewer resources, and ensure better governance without adding friction.
From summarizing board materials to monitoring compliance gaps and simplifying entity oversight, AI is starting to take root across the legal department.
They’re focused on applying AI where it can solve real, recurring problems — faster, more accurately, and securely.

kp.k: Board workflow automation could expand GCs’ strategic contribution
kp.d: The article presents AI integrated into board management software as a way to reduce preparation and follow-through work: compiling materials, flagging potential risks, summarizing content, preparing meeting questions, generating minutes and tracking actions. Cannon argues that this frees GCs to shape recommendations and improve board alignment. These are asserted capabilities and benefits, not quantified findings from an implementation study.
qs: Gathering past materials, formatting documents, cross-checking disclosures, and tracking action items often eats into time that should be spent shaping recommendations.
With purpose-built AI tools now integrated into board management software, legal teams can streamline how they build, review, and distribute board materials — without sacrificing control.
Surface potential legal and regulatory risks before materials are distributed
Track changes, generate minutes, and monitor follow-ups with transparency
With AI assisting in preparation and follow-through, legal leaders can help boards stay focused, aligned and informed.

kp.k: Entity management automation redirects effort toward advice and readiness
kp.d: Cannon describes automation of routine data entry, validation and formatting alongside AI-assisted retrieval and extraction of clauses, obligations and deadlines. She also describes updated organizational charts and faster, less error-prone audit reporting. The claimed consequence is less time gathering information and more time advising leadership, preparing transactions and maintaining regulatory readiness; no measured improvement is supplied.
qs: They need structured, accurate, and accessible entity data — and that’s where AI is proving transformative.
With automation handling routine data entry, validation, and document formatting, and AI surfacing key information in seconds, legal teams can:
Automatically extract key clauses, obligations, and deadlines from documents
For GCs, this means less time chasing details — and more time advising leadership, preparing for transactions, and ensuring regulatory readiness.

kp.k: AI is framed as augmentation rather than team replacement
kp.d: Cannon explicitly frames AI as making legal teams more effective rather than replacing them. Her proposed mechanism is automating repetitive or time-sensitive work to release capacity for thinking, analysis and advice. The article asserts improvements in contribution quality, speed and confidence, but does not provide staffing data or measured productivity outcomes.
qs: AI isn’t replacing legal teams — it’s making them more effective
Automating the parts of the job that are repetitive or time-sensitive — and freeing up time for deeper thinking, analysis, and advice.
Whether it's preparing the board for a critical vote or supporting an internal compliance review, GCs are using AI to improve the quality, speed, and confidence of their contributions.

kp.k: GCs should lead incremental, secure, outcome-focused adoption
kp.d: Cannon recommends that GCs shape organizational AI adoption around clear outcomes and security rather than attempt an immediate operational overhaul. She proposes starting with board preparation, compliance tracking or entity reporting and expanding from there, positioning the GC as an adoption leader rather than solely an adviser.
qs: GCs are in a unique position to shape how their organizations adopt AI: thoughtfully, securely, and with clear outcomes in mind.
This doesn’t mean legal teams need to overhaul their operations overnight.
It means starting where AI can help most — board preparation, compliance tracking, or entity reporting — and building from there.
With the right tools and the right approach, GCs are proving they’re not just advisors to AI adoption. They’re leading it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Cannon presents AI as an already-emerging tool for corporate legal departments that improves governance, entity management and compliance while expanding GCs’ strategic contribution rather than replacing legal teams.
pts.d: Hope Cannon makes four connected claims. First, purpose-built AI in board management software streamlines compiling, formatting, reviewing and distributing board materials, identifies potential legal and regulatory risks, summarizes content, personalizes meeting preparation, and supports minutes and follow-ups. She argues this frees GCs to shape recommendations and exert greater influence on boards. Second, AI-powered entity management combines routine automation with AI-assisted information retrieval and extraction to improve access to corporate records, identify clauses and deadlines, maintain organizational charts, and produce faster, less error-prone audit reporting. She links these efficiencies to more time for leadership advice, transactions and regulatory readiness. Third, she explicitly frames AI as augmentation: repetitive or time-sensitive work is automated so legal teams can focus on analysis and advice, improving the quality, speed and confidence of their contributions. Fourth, she argues that GCs are becoming leaders of organizational AI adoption, not merely advisers to it. These are claims about in-house legal and governance functions, not predictions about law-firm staffing, legal-market pricing or access to justice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article cites survey figures for adoption and technology planning, while supporting its operational-benefit claims with descriptions of Diligent products rather than measured outcomes.
pts.d: Cannon cites FTI Consulting’s The General Counsel Report 2025 for the statements that more than two-thirds of GCs are open to generative AI for major legal use cases, nearly half report already using it, and three-quarters of legal departments lack a technology roadmap. The article does not give the survey sample, methodology or fieldwork dates. These figures establish the reported adoption and planning context; they do not measure the asserted improvements in efficiency, accuracy, risk reduction or strategic influence. For those benefits, Cannon offers feature descriptions of Diligent Boards’ GovernAI suite and Diligent Entities. The source is a Diligent article by a director of legal operations and includes promotional calls to action for these workflows. It supplies no named customer cases, quantified time savings, comparative performance tests, accuracy measurements or employment data supporting the non-replacement claim.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Benefits are presented as occurring already as of May 23, 2025; wider adoption is framed as incremental and conditional on suitable tools, security, control and clear objectives.
pts.d: Cannon uses present-tense language such as 'now integrated,' 'starting to take root' and 'already delivering value,' rather than setting a future deployment deadline. The cited adoption report is labeled 2025, but the article gives no more precise data period. For continued adoption, she recommends starting with recurring problems in board preparation, compliance tracking or entity reporting and expanding from there. She qualifies the benefit claims by noting that tools differ and emphasizing purpose-built governance and legal workflows, secure implementation, clear outcomes and leadership. Human legal teams remain responsible for higher-level analysis and advice in this framing; the article does not specify an output-verification protocol or predict a date for autonomous legal work.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are GCs and corporate legal departments, with downstream benefits claimed for governance teams, boards and corporate leadership.
pts.d: GCs are portrayed as facing more regulatory complexity, resource pressure and board expectations; AI is said to reduce administrative demands and increase their capacity for strategic advice and organizational AI leadership. In-house legal and compliance teams gain faster retrieval and maintenance of entity information, automated document processing and improved reporting. Wider governance teams receive assistance preparing board materials and tracking meeting actions. Boards are said to become better informed and aligned, while corporate leadership receives more legal attention to transactions and regulatory readiness. Diligent appears as a software vendor supplying the featured tools, not as an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work. The article does not identify effects on outside counsel, junior-lawyer recruitment, legal fees or individuals with unmet legal needs.
